lessons.summary: Analyse how spoken address uses rhythm, repetition and audience relationship while separating script from performance.
objectives: Explain direct address and repetition.
Track a speech’s movement towards action.
Distinguish written evidence from unavailable delivery evidence.
explanation: A speech is shaped for listeners in a particular setting. Direct address, repeated phrases and signposted transitions can help an audience follow an argument as it unfolds. Examine how pronouns define a group: “we” may create shared responsibility, but its boundaries depend on context. Repetition can give a sequence emphasis or rhythm; explain what is repeated and how the surrounding ideas develop instead of simply naming the device.

A transcript records words and sometimes delivery notes, but it cannot alone establish pace, accent, volume, gesture or audience reaction. Use those features only when a recording or reliable direction supplies them. Track the relationship between opening, development and conclusion. A speech might begin with a shared concern, acknowledge a difficulty and end in a specific request. Such a structure invites participation without proving that listeners agree.
keyIdeas: Listeners encounter an unfolding sequence.
Pronouns construct a relationship with the audience.
Delivery claims require delivery evidence.

definitions.meaning: Language that explicitly speaks to an audience.
Repetition at the beginnings of successive clauses or phrases.
A request for the audience to do something specific.

method: Establish the supplied speaker, listeners and occasion.
Mark repetition, pronouns and transitions.
Trace how the sequence prepares the request.
Limit delivery claims to available evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original student speech to classmates: “We share these corridors. We share the noise. Let us share the work of keeping one room quiet.”
steps: Repeated “We share” establishes common experience and gives the opening parallel structure.
The move from corridors and noise to “work” changes shared experience into shared responsibility.
“Let us” invites collective action towards the specific quiet-room goal.
workedExample.conclusion: The speech builds a request from familiar communal experience. The transcript supports a pattern of repetition, but gives no evidence of actual applause or vocal volume.

misconceptions.mistake: Inventing a shouted delivery from an exclamation or urgent phrase.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the wording; qualify performance unless supplied.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating “we” as proof of genuine agreement.
misconceptions.correction: Explain the group the speaker attempts to construct.

practice.prompt: Explain the direct address in this original speech opening: “You have waited for an answer. Today, I can give you a date.”
hints: How are listeners placed in the situation?
solution: “You” recognises the listeners as people who have waited.
The shift to “I” presents the speaker as able to respond with a concrete date.

practice.prompt: Analyse the progression in the original line “We asked for a path. We planned a path. Now we must build it.”
hints: Compare the verbs and final obligation.
solution: “Asked” and “planned” mark earlier stages, while repeated syntax connects them.
“Now” moves to the present and “must” makes action an obligation.
The sequence frames building as the next step, though it does not establish agreement or resources.

practice.prompt: A transcript says “Please stay and help.” An analysis claims the speaker whispered and made every listener feel guilty. Evaluate both claims.
hints: Separate possible readings from observed delivery and response.
solution: No supplied delivery note establishes whispering.
“Please” makes a polite appeal, which may invite a sense of responsibility.
Every listener’s guilt cannot be inferred from the words; state a possible effect rather than a universal reaction.

practice.prompt: Original speech: “First, listen. Next, record the problem. Finally, agree a response.” Explain its suitability for spoken instructions.
solution: First, next and finally mark an audible order.
Each short sentence contains one main action.
The structure helps listeners retain the procedure without rereading a long sentence.
successCriteria: First, next and finally mark an audible order.
Each short sentence contains one main action.
The structure helps listeners retain the procedure without rereading a long sentence.

practice.prompt: Original speech says “We all have spare time after school.” Evaluate the inclusive pronoun.
hints: Consider a listener with caring duties.
solution: “We” attempts to unite the audience.
“All” assumes every listener has the same availability.
Listeners with work, journeys or caring duties may be excluded, so the claim needs qualification.
successCriteria: “All” assumes every listener has the same availability.
Listeners with work, journeys or caring duties may be excluded, so the claim needs qualification.

notes.title: Speeches in context
paragraphs: A speech is heard over time, so signposting and repetition can help listeners follow an argument they cannot easily reread. Pronouns establish relationships: we may invite solidarity, but it can also assume agreement. Pauses, sentence length and direct address can shape emphasis when performance details are supplied. Analyse the words separately from any invented delivery. A speech to classmates may draw on shared experience, whereas a public audience may need more context. Consider who is included in an appeal and whose different circumstances complicate it.

workedExamples.prompt: Original school speech: “Some of us arrive early. Some arrive after long journeys. All of us need a place to begin calmly.” Analyse the inclusive appeal.
steps: The first two sentences acknowledge different routines through repeated structure.
“All of us” then joins those differences around a common need.
workedExamples.conclusion: The speech builds inclusion by recognising unequal circumstances before proposing shared support.

flashcards.front: Why is signposting useful in speech?
flashcards.back: Listeners need to follow an argument as it unfolds in real time.
A shared identity or agreement, which may need examination.
When it is observed or supplied, not merely imagined.

flashcards.front: How does repeated syntax aid listening?
flashcards.back: It makes relationships between successive points easier to recognise.

diagrams.title: Speeches: relationships to explain

nodes.label: Different journeys
nodes.detail: The audience does not arrive in one way.

nodes.label: Common need
nodes.detail: A calm start becomes a shared concern.

edges.label: Parallel phrasing acknowledges both situations.
The shift to “all” connects difference with common purpose.

lessons.summary: Analyse how an advertisement presents a benefit, constructs an audience and qualifies its offer.
objectives: Connect an advertised benefit to an intended audience.
Read prominent claims alongside conditions.
Separate positioning from verified product performance.
explanation: Advertisements select features and benefits to make an offer attractive to an audience. A feature describes the product; a benefit frames what that feature could mean to a user. Analyse the relationship among headline, image, explanatory copy and call to action when those elements are supplied. Prominence can direct attention, but visual emphasis does not make a claim more accurate. A description of a layout is sufficient evidence for analysis only of the features it actually specifies.

Conditions can significantly narrow a headline promise. Read a price alongside its duration, eligibility and extra charges, or a performance claim alongside its stated testing conditions. Do not invent endorsements or data that the advertisement omits. A persuasive choice may associate a product with freedom, belonging or efficiency without proving that buyers will experience those outcomes. Distinguish the invitation to imagine a benefit from independent evidence of that benefit.
keyIdeas: Features are framed as benefits.
Prominence and qualification work together.
An advertisement is evidence of a claim, not automatic proof of it.

definitions.meaning: The value a feature is presented as offering a user.
A concise phrase intended to make an offer or identity memorable.
A condition or limit attached to a claim.

method: Identify the supplied offer and audience cues.
Connect headline and design to a promised benefit.
Read conditions and omissions.
Evaluate the positioning without inventing performance evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original advert description: a large headline says “Your desk, anywhere”; a smaller line says “Foldable desk. Indoor use on level surfaces.” The button says “See dimensions”.
steps: “Anywhere” initially suggests freedom from a fixed workspace.
The smaller conditions limit the claim to indoor, level surfaces.
“See dimensions” invites a practical suitability check, rather than immediate purchase.
workedExample.conclusion: The advert combines an expansive benefit with narrower usage conditions. A responsible reading includes both and does not treat “anywhere” literally.

misconceptions.mistake: Ignoring small-print conditions.
misconceptions.correction: Read the offer as a whole.

misconceptions.mistake: Claiming an image proves the product’s performance.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish presentation from test evidence.

practice.prompt: In the original advert “A 500 ml bottle that fits your bag”, distinguish a feature from a claimed benefit.
solution: The 500 ml capacity is a feature.
Fitting a bag is presented as a portability benefit, though actual fit depends on the bag.

practice.prompt: An original advert shows “Free delivery” prominently and “Orders over £30” beneath it. Analyse the relationship.
hints: Does the condition apply to every order?
solution: The prominent phrase foregrounds a saving.
The condition restricts eligibility to orders over £30.
Quoting the headline alone would imply a broader offer than the full text provides.

practice.prompt: An original poster claims “The notebook of successful people” without evidence. Explain the appeal and its evidential limit.
solution: It associates ownership with success and may appeal to aspiration.
The wording supplies no definition or evidence of success.
Even evidence that successful people use it would not establish that it causes success.

practice.prompt: Original advert: “Fits your day.” Details: “Notebook with 80 pages, A5 size.” Separate emotional appeal from measurable information.
hints: Which words can be checked directly?
solution: “Fits your day” suggests convenience or flexibility.
Eighty pages and A5 size are measurable specifications.
The slogan alone does not establish that the notebook suits every person’s routine.
successCriteria: “Fits your day” suggests convenience or flexibility.
Eighty pages and A5 size are measurable specifications.
The slogan alone does not establish that the notebook suits every person’s routine.

practice.prompt: A fictional advert shows one happy user and says “Join thousands”. What can and cannot be concluded?
hints: What does the number refer to?
solution: The image presents a positive experience for one depicted user.
“Join thousands” claims a large group without specifying satisfaction or results.
Neither element establishes that every purchaser will have the same experience.
successCriteria: The image presents a positive experience for one depicted user.
“Join thousands” claims a large group without specifying satisfaction or results.
Neither element establishes that every purchaser will have the same experience.

checklist: I avoid treating promotion as verification.

notes.title: Advertisements in context
paragraphs: Advertisements direct attention towards a response, but their appeal and their verifiable product claims should be examined separately. A large headline may create an emotional promise while smaller text limits the conditions. Analyse the hierarchy between image, slogan, description and call to action. Consider what information a reader needs to judge the offer, without assuming that missing information proves deception. For invented classroom adverts, describe the supplied design accurately and distinguish what is shown from what the advert merely invites the viewer to imagine.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional advert: “A quieter corner.” Beneath a photograph of a desk screen, small text reads “Reduces visual distraction; does not block sound.” The button says “Check measurements”. Analyse the claim.
steps: The headline suggests calm broadly, but the small print limits the product to visual distraction.
The measurements button directs readers to check suitability rather than assuming the screen fits every desk.
workedExamples.conclusion: The advert combines an emotional appeal with a narrower practical description that should govern the reader’s expectations.

flashcards.front: What is a call to action?
flashcards.back: The response an advert explicitly invites, such as checking details or ordering.

flashcards.front: Why compare headline and small print?
flashcards.back: Their scope may differ, changing what is actually promised.
The relative prominence of elements that guides attention.

flashcards.front: Does an appealing image prove a product works?
flashcards.back: No; it can suggest a desirable experience without demonstrating performance.

diagrams.title: Advertisements: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Headline → Qualification → Reader action. The practical limit makes fit relevant to the decision.

nodes.label: Qualification
nodes.detail: The screen affects sight, not sound.

nodes.label: Reader action
nodes.detail: Check dimensions for the actual setting.

edges.label: Small print narrows the broad impression.
The practical limit makes fit relevant to the decision.

lessons.summary: Analyse how an article frames a topic through its headline, lead, sources and organisation.
objectives: Compare a headline with the article’s scope.
Distinguish reporting, attribution and comment.
Evaluate selection and balance using supplied evidence.
explanation: An article organises information for a particular readership and purpose. Its headline and opening, often called the lead, establish a frame before later detail develops or qualifies it. Compare their emphasis with the body: an attention-grabbing summary can narrow a complex issue or overstate a tentative finding. Different article types permit different voices; a reported feature and an opinion column need not use the same style or claim the same neutrality.

Attribution identifies who is responsible for a statement. “The organiser said” records a claim without independently verifying it. Consider which perspectives are included, which evidence is supplied and whether the text distinguishes observation from opinion. Balance does not require treating every unsupported claim as equally credible. Analyse the information available, explaining omissions as limits of the supplied passage rather than inventing what the full publication contains.
keyIdeas: Opening emphasis frames later detail.
Attribution preserves responsibility for claims.
Variety of voices and quality of evidence are different questions.

definitions.meaning: The opening of an article that establishes its main focus.
Identification of the source of a statement.
The viewpoint expressed through comment or selection and framing.

method: Identify article type and supplied audience.
Compare headline and lead with detail.
Track sources and distinguish comment from reporting.
Evaluate how selection shapes the account.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original article extract. Headline: “Park plan wins backing”. Body: “At Tuesday’s meeting, six of the ten attendees supported the plan. The organiser called it a strong start. No wider survey has been held.”
steps: The headline foregrounds support but does not state its scale.
The body narrows that support to six meeting attendees.
“Strong start” is attributed to the organiser; the final sentence limits claims about wider opinion.
workedExample.conclusion: The body qualifies the headline and separates an interested person’s judgement from the reported count. It does not establish the views of the wider community.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating an attributed claim as verified fact.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the speaker and examine support.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming one omitted perspective proves deliberate deception.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the limitation without claiming an unsupported motive.

practice.prompt: In the original sentence “The coach called the result encouraging”, identify whose judgement “encouraging” expresses.
solution: It expresses the coach’s reported judgement.
The sentence does not by itself establish that the writer shares that judgement.

practice.prompt: Compare the original headline “Travel times fall” with the body “The average fell on two routes during one quiet week.”
solution: The headline presents a broad trend.
The body limits the observation to two routes and a particular week.
A careful analysis retains those limits rather than generalising to all routes or weeks.

practice.prompt: An original article about a school club quotes its leader and lists meeting times, but gives no member views. Evaluate what it supports and what remains uncertain.
hints: Avoid inventing why views were omitted.
solution: It can communicate the leader’s account and practical schedule.
It gives limited evidence about members’ experiences or agreement.
The omission limits that aspect of the account, but does not prove a deliberate attempt to silence members.

practice.prompt: Original article: “The organiser called the event a success; no attendance figures were released.” What kind of evidence is supplied?
solution: Success is the organiser’s attributed judgement.
No attendance figures are provided to assess that dimension independently.
The sentence supports a claim about the organiser’s view, not an established measure of overall success.
successCriteria: Success is the organiser’s attributed judgement.
No attendance figures are provided to assess that dimension independently.
The sentence supports a claim about the organiser’s view, not an established measure of overall success.

practice.prompt: A headline says “Most residents agree”, but the body reports 18 of 20 people at a supporters’ meeting. Evaluate.
hints: Inspect how the group was selected.
solution: Eighteen of twenty is most of the meeting attendees.
A supporters’ meeting is not necessarily representative of all residents.
The headline broadens the finding beyond the group actually surveyed.
successCriteria: Eighteen of twenty is most of the meeting attendees.
A supporters’ meeting is not necessarily representative of all residents.
The headline broadens the finding beyond the group actually surveyed.

notes.title: Articles in context
paragraphs: An article can report events while framing their significance through headlines, ordering and source selection. Distinguish the reporter’s statement from an attributed opinion. A quotation establishes that someone made a claim, not automatically that the claim is true. Numbers need denominators, time periods and relevant comparisons. The first paragraph often gives prominence to one interpretation; later qualifications may narrow it. Analyse these relationships without assuming that every difference in emphasis is deliberate deception.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional article: headline “Visitors double”; body “The exhibition received 40 visitors this Saturday, compared with 20 on the previous rainy Saturday.” Evaluate the framing.
steps: 40 is twice 20, so the headline accurately expresses the numerical change.
The comparison covers only two Saturdays and includes a difference in weather.
workedExamples.conclusion: The headline is numerically correct, but it cannot establish a lasting trend or identify what caused the increase.

flashcards.back: Who made a statement or supplied information.
A percentage or proportion is meaningful only in relation to its base.

flashcards.front: What can a quotation establish directly?
flashcards.back: That the attributed person made the stated claim, subject to accurate reporting.
Later details may qualify the scope or certainty of its framing.

diagrams.title: Articles: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Headline → Underlying figures → Bounded conclusion. Context limits the inference drawn from the change.

nodes.label: Bounded conclusion
nodes.detail: A two-day comparison, not a proven trend.

edges.label: The headline compresses the numbers.
Context limits the inference drawn from the change.

lessons.summary: Explain how composition, scale and relationships between words and images guide interpretation.
objectives: Describe visible features before interpreting.
Connect hierarchy and placement to emphasis.
Avoid universal claims about colours and symbols.
explanation: Visual texts arrange elements so that relationships become meaningful. Describe placement, relative size, contrast, gaze or framing only when the image or its supplied description provides them. Visual hierarchy can make one element more noticeable than another. Explain how this emphasis relates to the text’s purpose and context; do not assume that every viewer follows exactly the same viewing path or interprets every colour in the same way.

Words can anchor an image by narrowing its possible meanings, while an image can complicate or extend written language. Compare the contributions of each mode instead of treating the picture as decoration. A cropped image leaves information outside the frame, but the analyst cannot recover that information without evidence. These exercises use complete original layout descriptions; discuss their specified features without pretending to have observed an actual photograph or inventing extra visual details.
keyIdeas: Description comes before interpretation.
Relative scale and placement create emphasis.
Text can narrow an image’s possible meanings.

definitions.meaning: The arrangement and relationship of elements in an image or layout.
Relative prominence created through features such as size, position and contrast.
Words directing an audience towards a particular interpretation of an image.

method: List the supplied visible features.
Identify the most prominent relationships.
Connect words and images to context.
Qualify interpretation and acknowledge unseen information.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original poster description: a large empty chair occupies the centre; beneath it, smaller text reads “A place for every learner”. No people are shown.
steps: The central scale gives the chair visual prominence.
The caption connects a literal place to inclusion in learning.
The absence of people leaves the intended occupant unspecified, which can invite a broad audience to imagine belonging.
workedExample.conclusion: The supplied composition supports a reading about inclusion. It does not identify a particular absent pupil or establish an actual shortage of chairs.

misconceptions.mistake: Assigning one fixed meaning to a colour everywhere.
misconceptions.correction: Use the local context and acknowledge alternatives.

misconceptions.mistake: Inventing detail outside a crop.
misconceptions.correction: State what is excluded or unknown without reconstructing it.

practice.prompt: An original poster description places a large “JOIN” above a much smaller date. Explain one effect of this hierarchy.
solution: The larger invitation foregrounds action.
The smaller date supplies supporting information but may attract less immediate attention.

practice.prompt: An original image description shows two hands repairing a torn page. The caption is “Keep the story going”. Analyse their relationship.
hints: How does the wording extend the repair?
solution: The hands and tear present a concrete act of repair.
“Story” can connect preserving the physical page to preserving its narrative.
The caption frames the repair as continuity, without identifying who owns the book.

practice.prompt: A response says an original blue poster must make every viewer calm. Evaluate the claim using only the supplied colour.
solution: Blue is an observable feature, but its significance depends on context and viewer associations.
No layout, wording or audience evidence establishes a universal calming effect.
A responsible analysis would request or use additional supplied features and phrase any emotional effect as a possibility.

practice.prompt: Original poster: three equal-sized circles are separated; a line connects only two. Text: “Who is missing?” Analyse a plausible effect.
solution: The equal size presents the circles as comparable.
The unconnected third circle becomes conspicuous through the missing line.
The question invites reflection on exclusion rather than proving whom the circles represent.
successCriteria: The equal size presents the circles as comparable.
The unconnected third circle becomes conspicuous through the missing line.
The question invites reflection on exclusion rather than proving whom the circles represent.

practice.prompt: A supplied image description mentions monochrome shapes only. A response analyses a red background. Explain the error and repair.
solution: The response invents a colour absent from the description.
Its interpretation therefore rests on unsupported evidence.
Analyse the stated monochrome contrast, shape or placement instead.
successCriteria: The response invents a colour absent from the description.
Its interpretation therefore rests on unsupported evidence.
Analyse the stated monochrome contrast, shape or placement instead.

notes.title: Visual texts in context
paragraphs: Visual analysis begins with observable relationships: size, position, colour contrast, framing and the direction of attention. Explain how these choices interact rather than assigning a fixed meaning to each colour or shape. Written words can anchor an image’s interpretation, while an image can complicate a slogan. Distinguish a supplied description from features that are not shown. A large object may gain salience without symbolising power in every context. Keep cultural meanings and audience responses provisional unless reliable contextual evidence supports them.

workedExamples.prompt: Original poster description: a small seedling stands in the lower corner; a large watering can tilts towards it. Text reads “Small starts need support.” Analyse image and words together.
steps: The difference in size and the can’s direction make the seedling appear dependent on care.
The slogan guides the literal plant image towards a broader idea about helping beginnings develop.
workedExamples.conclusion: Text and composition work together to present support as an active relationship rather than an isolated quality of the seedling.

flashcards.back: The prominence that draws attention to an element.
Associations vary with context, culture and surrounding choices.

flashcards.front: How can text anchor an image?
flashcards.back: It directs attention towards a particular interpretation.
What is included, excluded and emphasised within the view.

diagrams.title: Visual texts: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Composition → Caption → Interpretation. Image and words jointly support the broader reading.

nodes.label: Composition
nodes.detail: A large can points towards a small plant.

nodes.label: Interpretation
nodes.detail: Care connects a beginning to growth.

edges.label: The caption gives the size relationship a conceptual focus.
Image and words jointly support the broader reading.

lessons.summary: Read how lineation, sound, imagery and shifts work together in a poem.
objectives: Distinguish speaker from author.
Explain a line break using its context.
Develop an interpretation through connected details.
explanation: Poetry uses language arranged in lines, although forms vary widely. A line ending can coincide with a grammatical pause or cut across a continuing phrase. Enjambment carries syntax beyond the line break; its effect depends on the words before and after the break. Read both the sentence and the line arrangement. Sound patterns, rhythm and repetition also matter, but identifying a device is only the start of explaining what it contributes.

Treat a poem’s speaker as a voice constructed within the text, not automatically the poet speaking autobiographically. Track images, changes in address and shifts of tone before proposing a theme. A short poem may leave its situation unresolved or support more than one reading. In the original examples below, a slash marks a line break. Quotations must preserve the actual words and analysis should explain patterns rather than force every detail into a single hidden message.
keyIdeas: Line and sentence boundaries can differ.
The speaker is not automatically the poet.
Patterns and shifts support interpretation.

definitions.meaning: Continuation of a grammatical phrase beyond a line ending.
A line ending at a clear grammatical pause or completion.
The voice speaking within a poem.

method: Read the whole poem for its situation.
Track line endings alongside syntax.
Connect sound or imagery to a shift.
Support a qualified interpretation with precise details.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original two-line poem, with / marking the break: “I kept the door open / for the sound of your key.”
steps: The first line initially presents the action of keeping a door open.
The second line completes its purpose, directing attention towards an anticipated sound.
The key links entry to an absent “you”, suggesting expectation without explaining the relationship or delay.
workedExample.conclusion: The break lets an ordinary action develop into an act of waiting. The text supports anticipation, but does not establish death, abandonment or the poet’s own experience.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every poem’s speaker the poet.
misconceptions.correction: Use “speaker” unless biographical identity is established.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying every short line creates the same effect.
misconceptions.correction: Explain the relationship between the break, syntax and content.

practice.prompt: In this original poem, “The rain stopped. / We stayed.”, explain how the line ending relates to grammar.
solution: Each line ends with a complete sentence and full stop, so the lines are end-stopped.
The separation gives the continued staying its own compact statement.

practice.prompt: Analyse the contrast in this original poem: “The station emptied / but your song filled my coat.”
hints: Consider physical space and figurative presence.
solution: “Emptied” presents departure or loss from the station.
The song figuratively “filled” the coat, suggesting sound or memory remaining close to the speaker.
The contrast makes absence coexist with a form of presence; the relationship and cause of separation remain unspecified.

practice.prompt: A reading of “At dawn I folded the map / and followed the river” says the poet rejects all planning forever. Evaluate and revise it.
hints: How far does this particular action support the claim?
solution: The speaker folds the map and follows the river at this moment; folding does not establish that the map is put away.
The words do not establish the poet’s personal beliefs or an enduring rejection of every plan.
The action may suggest greater attention to the river, without ruling out continued map use.

practice.prompt: Original poem: “The rain rehearsed / its answer on the roof.” Explain the personification and effect of the break.
hints: What human action is given to rain?
solution: “Rehearsed” gives rain a purposeful human activity.
The break delays what it rehearses: an “answer”.
The wording may make the repeated sound seem like speech being prepared rather than random noise.
successCriteria: “Rehearsed” gives rain a purposeful human activity.
The break delays what it rehearses: an “answer”.
The wording may make the repeated sound seem like speech being prepared rather than random noise.

practice.prompt: Original line: “Home, home, the sign insisted.” Explain why repetition alone does not prove comfort.
hints: Who or what repeats the word?
solution: Repeating “home” emphasises the idea of belonging.
“Insisted” can suggest pressure or a claim that needs defending.
The line may therefore question comfort as well as evoke it; wider context would help decide.
successCriteria: Repeating “home” emphasises the idea of belonging.
“Insisted” can suggest pressure or a claim that needs defending.
The line may therefore question comfort as well as evoke it; wider context would help decide.

notes.title: Poetry in context
paragraphs: Poetry can make meaning through the interaction of image, sound, syntax and lineation. A line break may delay completion, isolate a word or create a temporary reading that the next line revises. Do not assume a pause at every break; punctuation and grammar also shape reading. The speaker is a constructed voice, and the poem need not be autobiographical. Analyse how a feature works in this poem rather than attaching a standard emotion to rhyme or a short line. Where alternatives remain possible, explain the evidence for each.

workedExamples.prompt: Original two-line poem: “I left the window open / to a season that had gone.” Analyse the line break and image.
steps: The first line establishes a literal action and an expectation that something may enter.
The second line supplies an absent season as the object of welcome, shifting the action towards longing for what cannot return in that moment.
workedExamples.conclusion: The delayed completion turns an ordinary open window into an image of attachment to an absent time.

flashcards.back: The continuation of syntax beyond a line break without a full grammatical stop.

flashcards.front: Is the poetic speaker necessarily the poet?
flashcards.back: No; the speaker is a voice constructed by the poem.

flashcards.front: Why read across a line break?
flashcards.back: The next line may complete or revise the meaning temporarily suggested.

flashcards.front: Does rhyme guarantee a cheerful tone?
flashcards.back: No; sound patterns interact with subject, wording and structure.

diagrams.title: Poetry: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: First line → Second line → Revised meaning. Completion changes how the opening is understood.

nodes.label: Second line
nodes.detail: The welcome is directed to an absent season.

nodes.label: Revised meaning
nodes.detail: A literal action becomes an image of longing.

edges.label: The break delays what the window is opened to.
Completion changes how the opening is understood.

lessons.summary: Analyse narrative perspective, characterisation and pace without confusing narrator and author.
objectives: Identify what a narrative voice can know.
Infer character from supplied actions and language.
Explain a change in narrative pace.
explanation: Prose narrative presents events through a selected perspective. A first-person narrator takes part in or reports the story using “I”, but that grammatical position does not guarantee honesty or complete knowledge. Third-person narration may closely follow one character or range more broadly. Establish access to thoughts and events from the passage itself. Distinguish the author who constructs the narrative from the narrator whose voice presents it.

Characterisation can arise through action, speech, description and what others say. An inference about motivation should account for the evidence without inventing a complete past. Pace depends on how much narrative space an event receives: a brief action may be expanded through detail, while years can be summarised in a sentence. Explain how this allocation of attention shapes the reader’s encounter with an event rather than merely listing sentence lengths.
keyIdeas: Perspective limits or extends knowledge.
Actions support qualified character inferences.
Narrative time and reading space can differ.

definitions.meaning: The voice that tells a narrative.
The construction of a character through selected details.
The rate at which events are presented relative to the space given to them.

method: Identify the narrative position and knowledge.
Select actions or details relevant to the question.
Track where narration slows or summarises.
Connect perspective and pace to an interpretation.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original passage: “I called it an easy climb. At the first step, I checked the rope, then the knot, then the rope again.”
steps: The first-person narrator initially labels the climb “easy”.
The repeated checking contrasts with that confident label.
The step-by-step list slows a small moment, drawing attention to caution or unease.
workedExample.conclusion: The narrator’s actions complicate the confident description. Anxiety is a possible inference, though careful safety checking also fits the actions and should not be ruled out without further context.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating first person as automatic unreliability.
misconceptions.correction: Identify a specific inconsistency or limitation.

misconceptions.mistake: Diagnosing a character from one action.
misconceptions.correction: Offer a proportionate inference and consider alternatives.

practice.prompt: In “I watched Arun leave; I could not tell why he smiled”, identify one thing the narrator knows and one limit.
solution: The narrator observes Arun leaving and smiling.
The reason for the smile is explicitly unknown.

practice.prompt: Analyse the pace of this original passage: “For years the shop stayed closed. Today, she turned the key once, waited, and turned it again.”
hints: Compare years with the detailed present action.
solution: Years are compressed into one sentence.
The present action is divided into turning, waiting and repetition.
This slows attention around reopening and may make it feel significant or tentative.

practice.prompt: A response to “He returned the untouched meal and asked for water” claims the character dislikes the cook. Evaluate and propose an alternative reading.
hints: What motives are and are not supplied?
solution: Returning the meal and requesting water are given; dislike of the cook is not.
Illness, lack of appetite or another practical reason could fit, but none is established.
A defensible account describes refusal of this meal while leaving motive open.

practice.prompt: Original passage: “Mina smiled. I knew she forgave me.” Identify observation and inference.
hints: Can the narrator directly know forgiveness?
solution: Mina’s smile is the reported observable action.
Forgiveness is the narrator’s interpretation of it.
The smile alone may have other explanations, so the certainty of “knew” can be questioned.
successCriteria: Mina’s smile is the reported observable action.
Forgiveness is the narrator’s interpretation of it.

practice.prompt: A paragraph spends six sentences describing a hand approaching a door handle. Explain a likely structural effect without inventing the plot.
hints: Compare narrated time with reading time.

Extended description slows the reader’s attention and emphasises the approach.
This can build anticipation, but the reason for it must come from other supplied details.

notes.title: Prose in context
paragraphs: Prose narration controls access to information. A first-person narrator can describe private thoughts but cannot directly know another character’s mind without a stated basis. A third-person narrative may be limited to one perspective or move more broadly. Distinguish what happens from the narrator’s interpretation of it. Contradictions between a confident statement and observed behaviour can invite readers to question reliability. Pacing also matters: several sentences on a brief action can slow attention and reveal what the narration treats as significant.

workedExamples.prompt: Original passage: “I had forgotten the letter completely. I checked the drawer before breakfast, after lunch, and once more at dusk.” Analyse reliability.
steps: The opening claim says the narrator no longer remembers or thinks about the letter.
The three checks contradict that claim through repeated behaviour across the day.
workedExamples.conclusion: The discrepancy invites doubt about the narrator’s self-description, though it does not establish whether the misrepresentation is conscious.

flashcards.back: The position and limits from which events are presented.
Actions may contradict what the narrator claims about motives or feelings.
No; knowledge, memory and self-presentation can all be limited.
By devoting detailed description or several sentences to a brief moment.

lessons.summary: Analyse dialogue, stage directions and dramatic tension while allowing for different performances.
objectives: Distinguish spoken dialogue from stage directions.
Infer subtext from contradictions and pauses.
Explain what a script establishes and leaves to performance.
explanation: Drama is written for performance, so dialogue interacts with movement, space, silence and timing. Stage directions may specify an action or pause that changes how a spoken line can be understood. Read them as evidence alongside the words. A character’s statement need not be a transparent account of feelings: contradiction between speech and action can create subtext, the meaning implied beneath what is said.

A script allows choices for actors and directors unless it specifies delivery precisely. Distinguish a possible interpretation of a pause from a recorded performance fact. Dramatic irony occurs when an audience knows something a character does not; this requires supplied evidence of the knowledge difference. Tension can arise from delayed replies, competing aims or blocked actions without dramatic irony. Avoid inventing lighting, tone of voice or audience reactions absent from the extract.
keyIdeas: Action can complicate dialogue.
Subtext is inferred from evidence.
A performance choice is not automatically a script fact.

definitions.meaning: A script instruction or description concerning action or staging.
Meaning implied beneath the explicit words or actions.
A situation in which audience knowledge exceeds that of a character in a relevant way.

method: Separate dialogue and supplied directions.
Identify the characters’ stated aims.
Connect pauses or actions to tension or subtext.
Distinguish script evidence from possible performance choices.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse this original script: “LEA: I am ready. [She puts the suitcase down.] TOM: Then why are we still here?”
steps: Lea’s assertion of readiness contrasts with putting down the suitcase.
Tom’s question makes that mismatch explicit and presses for movement.
The action could suggest hesitation, but the script does not specify fear, anger or a particular delivery.
workedExample.conclusion: The exchange creates tension between declared readiness and delayed departure. A performance can develop that tension in different ways consistent with the words and action.

misconceptions.mistake: Inventing a director’s choice as textual evidence.
misconceptions.correction: Label a possible staging as a proposal.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling any surprising line dramatic irony.
misconceptions.correction: Show the audience/character knowledge gap.

practice.prompt: In the original script “SAM: Stay. [A pause.] Please.”, explain one possible function of the pause.
hints: Compare the command with the added appeal.
solution: The pause separates the initial command from the plea.
It may make “Please” sound like a reconsideration or more vulnerable appeal, depending on performance.

practice.prompt: Analyse this original exchange: “ARI: Take the last seat. [Ari remains standing beside it.] JO: You have been standing all day.”
hints: How does the reply complicate the offer?
solution: Ari offers the seat while remaining close to it.
Jo’s reply draws attention to Ari’s own possible need for rest.
The exchange can suggest consideration between the characters, without establishing either person’s hidden motive conclusively.

practice.prompt: A script extract says “MIA: The room is empty.” No other scene or direction is supplied. Can an analysis establish dramatic irony by claiming somebody hides inside?
hints: Is the audience given that knowledge?
solution: The extract supplies Mia’s claim but no evidence of a hidden person.
Dramatic irony cannot be established without the relevant audience knowledge.
A hidden person could be a proposed staging addition, but must not be reported as present in the supplied text.

practice.prompt: Original script: “AVA: Nothing has changed. [She removes a name card from the table.]” Analyse the contradiction.
solution: Ava denies change in her dialogue.
Removing a name card visibly alters who is represented at the table.
The contradiction may imply denial or concealment, without establishing the absent person’s story.
successCriteria: Ava denies change in her dialogue.

practice.prompt: A script supplies “[pause]” but no duration. Explain how two proposed performances could differ.
hints: Vary duration without inventing a specified fact.
Connect timing to a possible reading.
solution: A brief pause could suggest ordinary hesitation.
A longer pause could make avoidance or tension more noticeable.
These are performance interpretations; the script itself does not specify which duration is required.
successCriteria: A brief pause could suggest ordinary hesitation.

notes.title: Drama in context
paragraphs: Drama distributes meaning across dialogue, stage directions, pauses and relationships in space. Words may state one intention while movement suggests another, creating subtext. A script leaves some choices to performance, so distinguish specified actions from your proposed interpretation. Stage directions can shape what an audience sees, but they do not automatically reveal a character’s private thoughts. Analyse timing and entrances as well as language. When proposing a performance, explain how a choice could make a reading visible without claiming that every audience will respond identically.

workedExamples.prompt: Original script: “SAM: Take it. [He keeps his hand on the book.] ELI: Are you sure?” Analyse the conflict.
steps: The imperative offers the book verbally.
The retained hand prevents or complicates the transfer, and Eli’s question draws attention to the mismatch.
workedExamples.conclusion: The scene creates subtext of reluctance through the relationship between dialogue and action.

flashcards.back: An implied meaning or intention beneath the literal words.

flashcards.front: Why distinguish script from performance proposal?
flashcards.back: A proposed choice is an interpretation, not evidence already supplied.
Emphasis, pace or the apparent relationship between speakers.

flashcards.front: Do stage directions prove a private thought?
flashcards.back: No; they specify actions or conditions from which thoughts may be inferred.

lessons.summary: Build a comparative argument that explains meaningful relationships between texts rather than listing separate observations.
objectives: Choose a shared focus supported by both texts.
Connect similarities and differences to meaning.
Integrate evidence from both texts within a line of argument.
explanation: Comparison begins with a question that both texts can help answer. A useful point identifies a relationship: two speakers may both discuss a journey but differ in how much control they seem to have. Establish the common ground accurately before explaining a contrast. Use evidence from each text and give each detail enough analysis; adding “similarly” to two unrelated observations does not create a meaningful comparison.

Organise the response around ideas that advance the argument. A paragraph can move from a shared concern to different choices and their implications, while keeping each text’s context distinct. Similarity does not mean identical purpose, and difference does not require deciding that one text is better. Avoid forcing symmetry: one text may develop a concern more explicitly, and that imbalance can itself become a supported comparative point.
keyIdeas: A shared focus gives comparison direction.
Both texts need precise evidence.
Differences matter through their implications.

definitions.meaning: The question or idea used to relate two texts.
The supported common ground that makes a comparison meaningful.
A connected conclusion drawn from evidence considered together.

method: Choose a shared concern relevant to the task.
Select evidence from each text.
Explain the relationship and its implications.
Shape paragraphs around comparative claims.

workedExample.prompt: Compare control in these original lines. A: “I drew the route before we left.” B: “The road bent, and we went where it led.”
steps: Both lines describe movement along a route.
A foregrounds the narrator’s planning through “I drew”, while B gives the road apparent direction-setting agency.
The contrast suggests prepared control in A and responsive movement in B, without establishing the entire journeys.
workedExample.conclusion: Both address direction, but locate its source differently. The comparison remains local to the supplied lines rather than assigning permanent personalities to the travellers.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing two disconnected mini-essays.
misconceptions.correction: Use shared claims and explicit relationships.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming every comparison must rank quality.
misconceptions.correction: Explain differences relevant to the question.

practice.prompt: Compare the original invitations A: “Join us today” and B: “Consider joining when you can”.
solution: Both invite participation.
A uses an imperative and “today” for immediacy; B gives more room through “consider” and “when you can”.

practice.prompt: Compare waiting in A: “She counted every passing car” and B: “He let the afternoon drift past”, both original.
hints: How active is each response to time?
solution: Counting foregrounds repeated attention to events and can suggest alert anticipation.
“Let” and “drift” suggest a less directed experience of time.
Both concern passing time, but the language contrasts active monitoring with apparent acceptance; motives remain unspecified.

practice.prompt: Write a comparative claim about community from original A: “Our doors stand open” and B: “Knock, and someone will answer”. Include a limitation.
hints: Both permit contact, but on what terms?
solution: Both present access to others.
A depicts an already open boundary, while B makes a response follow an initial request.
A possible claim contrasts immediate openness with responsive welcome; neither line proves every person is actually included.

practice.prompt: Original lines: A, “The bell freed us.” B, “The bell sent us back.” Compare the bell’s function.
solution: Both lines give the bell power over movement or routine.
“Freed” frames it as release, while “sent us back” frames it as renewed obligation.
The contrast shows different experiences of the same kind of signal.
successCriteria: Both lines give the bell power over movement or routine.
“Freed” frames it as release, while “sent us back” frames it as renewed obligation.
The contrast shows different experiences of the same kind of signal.

practice.prompt: A comparison says only “Both texts use imagery.” Improve its analytical direction.
hints: Name a meaningful difference or similarity.
solution: Identify the specific images in each text.
Explain how each presents the shared theme.
State what their similarity or difference reveals, rather than stopping at a shared technique label.
successCriteria: Identify the specific images in each text.
Explain how each presents the shared theme.
State what their similarity or difference reveals, rather than stopping at a shared technique label.

notes.title: Comparative analysis in context
paragraphs: Comparison needs a shared basis: the same theme, relationship or technique considered in both texts. Organise around an argument about similarities and differences rather than writing two separate summaries. Similar imagery can serve different purposes, while different techniques can produce related effects. Use evidence from both texts in each major comparison where practical. Avoid ranking one as better unless the task supplies a relevant criterion. A useful comparative claim explains what the contrast reveals about the texts’ distinct presentations of the shared concern.

workedExamples.prompt: Original lines: A, “She locked the gate to keep the garden safe.” B, “He opened the gate so the garden could be shared.” Compare protection and access.
steps: Both lines connect a gate with decisions about the garden’s use.
A associates protection with restriction, while B associates value with participation.
workedExamples.conclusion: The shared object exposes different priorities: safety through control and benefit through access.

flashcards.front: What is a basis of comparison?
flashcards.back: A shared concern or feature considered across both texts.
They leave the reader to construct the comparison instead of explaining it.

flashcards.front: Can the same image have different functions?
flashcards.back: Yes; its wording, context and relationships determine its use.
When a relevant criterion and the task justify evaluation.

lessons.summary: Explain how selected language, perspective and form shape a text without claiming access to a writer’s private intentions.
objectives: Identify a specific choice at a useful scale.
Explain its mechanism in context.
Distinguish textual effect from proven authorial intention.
explanation: A text is made through choices about words, syntax, perspective, order and form. Analysis examines how these choices work together to guide attention or create possibilities of meaning. Select a detail relevant to the question rather than trying to catalogue every device. A useful explanation moves from what the text does to how it does it, then to a plausible significance supported by nearby evidence.

Calling something an authorial choice does not prove a conscious private intention. Phrase analysis in terms of what the text presents, foregrounds or invites unless reliable contextual evidence establishes a stated intention. Comparing a supplied phrase with a clearly labelled hypothetical alternative can clarify an effect, but the invented alternative must never be attributed to the original source. Consider how another choice might complicate the interpretation instead of treating one technique as decisive alone.
keyIdeas: Choices operate at several scales.
Mechanisms connect evidence to interpretation.
Effect and private intention are different claims.

definitions.meaning: The arrangement of words and clauses in sentences.
Making a feature or idea especially prominent.
What a writer meant to achieve, which is not directly observable from a text alone.

method: Select a choice relevant to the question.
Describe its precise operation.
Connect it to neighbouring evidence and meaning.
Qualify claims about intention or reception.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse the naming choice in this original passage: “The manager spoke. The manager signed. Only at the door did someone call her Asha.”
steps: The repeated role title initially defines the character through her position.
The personal name appears only in the final sentence.
This delayed naming shifts attention from institutional role towards individual identity.
workedExample.conclusion: The text foregrounds a change in how the character is addressed. It supports that effect without establishing why the writer personally chose it or how every reader responds.

misconceptions.mistake: Listing devices without explaining their operation.
misconceptions.correction: Connect a choice to a specific interpretive effect.

misconceptions.mistake: Claiming the writer definitely wanted a reaction without evidence.
misconceptions.correction: Describe an invitation or possible effect.

practice.prompt: Explain the repetition in the original line “Again she checked the lock. Again she checked the window.”
hints: Connect the repeated form and action.
solution: Repeated “Again” foregrounds recurrence.
The parallel actions can suggest persistent vigilance or concern, without naming its cause.

practice.prompt: Analyse the order in the original sentence “Before he answered, he counted the empty chairs.”
hints: What is delayed and what receives attention first?
solution: The opening delays the answer and places counting before speech.
The empty chairs become relevant to the moment of response.
The sequence can suggest that absence affects the answer, though the exact connection is not stated.

practice.prompt: A response says “The writer uses a short sentence because she hates crowded cities.” The only supplied sentence is “The street emptied.” Evaluate it.
solution: The sentence is brief and depicts a street becoming empty.
The writer’s gender and personal dislike are not supplied, and the sentence does not establish the setting as a city.
A better analysis explains how the compact statement foregrounds the change in occupancy, leaving attitude and motive open.

practice.prompt: Original passage calls a person “the customer” until the final word, “Dad”. Explain the effect of that naming change.
solution: “The customer” presents a public transactional role.
“Dad” introduces a personal relationship at the end.
The delayed recognition invites a rereading of the earlier interaction.
successCriteria: “The customer” presents a public transactional role.
“Dad” introduces a personal relationship at the end.
The delayed recognition invites a rereading of the earlier interaction.

practice.prompt: Explain why “the writer wanted everyone to feel angry” is too strong without further evidence.
hints: Check the claim about every reader.
solution: The statement claims private intention without evidence.
It also assumes a uniform audience response.
A stronger analysis identifies wording that may invite anger and explains why in this context.
successCriteria: The statement claims private intention without evidence.
It also assumes a uniform audience response.
A stronger analysis identifies wording that may invite anger and explains why in this context.

notes.title: Authorial choices in context
paragraphs: An authorial choice is a feature of how a text is made: selection of detail, voice, order, naming, syntax or omission. Analysis should show how a choice changes the information or associations available to a reader. You can compare the actual wording with a plausible alternative to clarify its effect, but the alternative is your analytical device, not another version of the text. Avoid claiming access to the author’s private intentions. Explain the function the choice performs in the supplied passage and consider how other choices reinforce or complicate it.

workedExamples.prompt: Original passage: “Someone knocked. Someone waited. At last, my brother called my name.” Analyse the delayed identification.
steps: Repeating “someone” withholds the visitor’s identity and creates uncertainty.
Naming “my brother” later changes the knock from an unknown event into a personal relationship.
workedExamples.conclusion: The delayed naming makes the reader experience uncertainty before recognition.

flashcards.front: What counts as an authorial choice?
flashcards.back: A decision about the text’s language, selection, arrangement or perspective.
It helps isolate what the actual choice contributes.

flashcards.front: Can an analysis establish private intention directly?
flashcards.back: Usually not; it can explain textual function and supported effects.
Withhold information, focus attention or preserve uncertainty.

lessons.summary: Infer a text’s attitude from patterns of language and recognise shifts or ambiguity.
objectives: Distinguish tone from atmosphere.
Support an attitude label with precise evidence.
Explain how a qualification or shift changes the tone.
explanation: Tone is the attitude conveyed by a voice towards its subject or audience. A label such as cautious, admiring or irritated needs support from diction, syntax and context. Mood or atmosphere concerns the feeling created by the scene or text; it is related to tone but is not identical. A speaker can describe an alarming event in a calm tone, producing a tension between subject and manner.

Track the voice across the passage rather than assigning one label permanently. A qualification may turn enthusiasm into caution, while a contrast between literal praise and context can support irony. Irony requires evidence of that contrast; punctuation or a positive adjective alone does not establish sarcasm. More than one tone may coexist. Explain how the evidence supports the chosen terms and recognise an alternative when the short passage leaves delivery or intention uncertain.
keyIdeas: Tone is an attitude conveyed through choices.
Atmosphere and tone can differ.
A voice may shift or combine attitudes.

definitions.meaning: The attitude a textual voice conveys towards a subject or audience.
The atmosphere or feeling a text can create.
A contrast between what is literally said and an implied meaning supported by context.

method: Identify the voice and its subject.
Choose a precise attitude label.
Support it with language patterns.
Track shifts and qualify ambiguous irony.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse the tone of this original comment: “The new path is welcome. If only it reached the bus stop.”
steps: “Welcome” explicitly approves the improvement.
“If only” introduces regret about a limitation.
The second sentence qualifies approval rather than cancelling every positive aspect.
workedExample.conclusion: The tone combines appreciation with disappointment. Calling it entirely celebratory or entirely hostile would ignore part of the wording.

misconceptions.mistake: Labelling a topic rather than an attitude.
misconceptions.correction: Explain how the voice responds to that topic.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling any praise sarcastic.
misconceptions.correction: Supply contextual evidence of a mismatch.

practice.prompt: Support a tone label for the original line “Perhaps we should check once more before deciding.”
solution: “Perhaps” makes the proposal tentative.
Checking before deciding supports a cautious tone rather than certainty.

practice.prompt: Analyse the tonal shift in “At last, a quiet room. Then the drilling began”, an original passage.
hints: Compare the expectation with the interruption.
solution: “At last” suggests relief at reaching quiet.
The drilling interrupts that expectation.
The sequence can imply frustration or wry disappointment, although the passage does not specify spoken delivery.

practice.prompt: An analysis calls “What a helpful map” sarcastic. No further context is supplied. Evaluate the certainty of that label.
solution: The literal wording expresses praise.
Sarcasm is possible in some contexts, but none is supplied to establish a mismatch.
The analysis should retain sincere praise as a possibility and qualify any ironic reading.

practice.prompt: Original comment: “A useful beginning, provided someone continues it.” Analyse its attitude.
solution: “Useful” gives the beginning value.
“Provided” makes that value conditional on continuation.
The tone is cautiously supportive rather than unreservedly enthusiastic.
successCriteria: “Provided” makes that value conditional on continuation.
The tone is cautiously supportive rather than unreservedly enthusiastic.

practice.prompt: Original comment: “Wonderful: another form to fill in.” Explain why context matters before calling it sarcastic.
hints: The adjective and situation may conflict.
Could the form be welcome in some contexts?
solution: “Wonderful” is literally positive.
If more forms are an unwanted burden, the contrast could imply sarcasm.
Without that context, a welcome opportunity requiring a form could make the statement sincere.
successCriteria: If more forms are an unwanted burden, the contrast could imply sarcasm.
Without that context, a welcome opportunity requiring a form could make the statement sincere.

notes.title: Tone in context
paragraphs: Tone is an attitude conveyed through language and form. It may be mixed or change within a sentence. Use a precise description such as restrained frustration, cautious optimism or dry amusement, then justify it with wording and structure. Do not infer tone solely from the topic: a serious event can be narrated ironically or with detachment. Irony requires a gap between literal wording and contextual meaning; a positive adjective is not automatically sarcastic. Track qualifications, punctuation and contrasts that revise an opening impression.

workedExamples.prompt: Original comment: “At last, a timetable we can read. Now we only need buses that follow it.” Analyse the tonal shift.
steps: The first sentence expresses relief through “At last”.
The second adds a practical failure, undercutting the apparent solution.
workedExamples.conclusion: The comment combines appreciation with dry frustration about the remaining problem.

flashcards.back: The attitude conveyed by wording and form towards the subject or audience.

flashcards.front: Why use a qualified tone label?
flashcards.back: A text may combine attitudes rather than express one simple emotion.

flashcards.front: What supports a claim of irony?
flashcards.back: A contextual gap between literal wording and implied meaning.

flashcards.front: Can subject matter alone determine tone?
flashcards.back: No; the same subject can be treated in very different ways.

lessons.summary: Explain how ordering, pace and shifts shape a reader’s changing understanding.
objectives: Map the progression of a passage.
Connect a shift to earlier details.
Explain delayed information without inventing its cause.
explanation: Structure concerns how a text arranges its parts and the relationships that arrangement creates. At a whole-text scale, consider openings, developments, turning points and endings. At a smaller scale, consider a list, a paragraph break or the placement of a final clause. A structural observation becomes analysis when it explains how the arrangement changes attention, expectation or understanding in this particular text.

Track what the reader knows at each stage. Delaying a detail can invite an early assumption that later evidence revises. Repetition can make a later variation significant, while a return to an opening image can create continuity or contrast. These patterns do not guarantee a single emotional response. Avoid vague claims that an ending is “effective”; show exactly what it recalls, reveals or leaves unresolved, and connect that movement to the question.
keyIdeas: Order shapes when information becomes available.
A shift gains meaning through what precedes it.
Returning to an image can change its significance.

definitions.meaning: A change in focus, time, voice or direction within a text.
Placing elements close together so their relationship becomes noticeable.
An arrangement that returns to an opening element or situation at the end.

method: Map the opening, development and ending.
Identify a significant change or return.
Explain what the reader knows before and after it.
Connect the movement to the task’s focus.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse the structure of this original passage: “The gate was locked. We searched the wall for a gap. At dusk, we found the key in our own bag.”
steps: The locked gate establishes an obstacle.
Searching the wall directs attention towards an external route around it.
The final discovery relocates the solution to something already carried, revising the earlier search.
workedExample.conclusion: The delayed key creates a contrast between effort directed outward and an overlooked resource nearby. The passage does not explain why the key was not found sooner.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling all final sentences a climax.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the particular change or resolution.

misconceptions.mistake: Listing beginning, middle and end without a relationship.
misconceptions.correction: Explain how later information develops or revises earlier details.

practice.prompt: In “The bell rang. No one moved. Then the door opened”, an original passage, identify a shift in action.
solution: “No one moved” establishes stillness after the bell.
“Then the door opened” introduces a new action and redirects attention to the doorway.

practice.prompt: An original passage opens “The desk was empty” and ends “The desk was empty, except for her letter”. Analyse the return.
solution: The ending repeats the opening image of emptiness.
The added exception introduces a trace of the character through the letter.
The return makes the new object significant against the otherwise unchanged space.

practice.prompt: A response says a surprise ending proves the narrator deliberately deceived the reader. The supplied passage only delays revealing a letter’s contents. Evaluate the claim.
hints: Is delayed narration the same as dishonest speech?
solution: Delayed disclosure is a structural choice.
It can create suspense or revise understanding without a narrator making a false statement.
Deliberate deception needs further evidence; analyse the delay and its effect separately from motive.

practice.prompt: Original passage opens “I would never return” and ends “I recognised the door before I reached it.” Explain the structural relationship.
hints: Compare the promise with the final location.
solution: The opening establishes a firm refusal.
The ending places the speaker back near a familiar door.
The contrast revises the opening certainty and invites questions about what caused the return.
successCriteria: The opening establishes a firm refusal.
The ending places the speaker back near a familiar door.
The contrast revises the opening certainty and invites questions about what caused the return.

practice.prompt: A narrative reveals only at the end that a letter was never posted. Explain how this can affect earlier scenes of waiting.
hints: What did readers assume about delivery?
solution: Earlier waiting may appear to anticipate a reply.
The final disclosure removes the assumed opportunity for the recipient to answer.
Readers may reinterpret the silence as a consequence of the unsent letter rather than rejection.
successCriteria: Earlier waiting may appear to anticipate a reply.
The final disclosure removes the assumed opportunity for the recipient to answer.
Readers may reinterpret the silence as a consequence of the unsent letter rather than rejection.

notes.title: Structure in context
paragraphs: Structure concerns the order and relationship of parts. An opening can establish an expectation that an ending fulfils, reverses or leaves unresolved. A return to an earlier object may show change even when the object itself stays the same. Analyse shifts in focus, chronology, pace and perspective, not only beginning, middle and end. Explain why information appears where it does: delayed knowledge can alter a reader’s judgement. Avoid assuming that a circular structure means nothing has changed; the returning detail may acquire a different significance.

workedExamples.prompt: Original miniature narrative: “At dawn, the chair was empty. All day we argued over who should sit there. At dusk, we carried it outside together.” Analyse the ending.
steps: The opening makes the empty chair a problem of possession or status.
The shared final action changes the focus from winning the seat to dealing with it collectively.
workedExamples.conclusion: The return to the chair creates continuity while the changed action suggests a revised relationship.

flashcards.back: How arrangement and relationships between parts contribute to meaning.
Change how earlier events or claims are understood.

flashcards.front: Does a returning object imply no change?
flashcards.back: No; a new context or action can transform its significance.
A meaningful change in focus, time, pace, perspective or pattern.

lessons.summary: Analyse the implications of particular words while preserving their local context and range of meanings.
objectives: Distinguish literal meaning from association.
Explain register and patterns of vocabulary.
Compare word choices without inventing a source quotation.
explanation: Diction is word choice. A word’s denotation is its literal or primary meaning in context, while its connotations are associations it can carry. Those associations depend on use and audience; a word need not suggest the same thing everywhere. Begin with what the word refers to, then explain how its associations contribute to the passage’s presentation of a person, object or event.

Consider patterns as well as individual words. Several terms drawn from finance, weather or conflict may establish a semantic field, but explain how that pattern shapes the subject. Register concerns the level or style of language appropriate to a situation, such as formal instruction or casual conversation. Comparing a source word with a clearly labelled alternative can sharpen analysis. Preserve the original wording and never present your substitute as a quotation from the passage.
keyIdeas: Meaning and association work together.
Vocabulary patterns can frame a subject.
A hypothetical substitute is an analytical tool, not source text.

definitions.meaning: The literal or primary meaning of a word in context.
An association a word may carry beyond its literal reference.
A style or level of language related to a situation and audience.

method: Quote the exact relevant word.
Establish its meaning in context.
Explain an association or vocabulary pattern.
Connect the choice to the passage’s portrayal.

workedExample.prompt: Analyse “clung” in this original sentence: “He clung to the timetable as the announcements changed.”
steps: “Clung” literally suggests holding tightly and can imply dependence or reluctance to let go.
The changing announcements contrast with reliance on the fixed timetable.
Compared with the hypothetical neutral alternative “held”, “clung” gives the attachment greater intensity.
workedExample.conclusion: The choice can present the timetable as a source of security amid uncertainty. It does not prove a particular emotional diagnosis.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming a dictionary definition completes analysis.
misconceptions.correction: Explain the word’s function in this passage.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating every association as universal.
misconceptions.correction: Qualify it through local evidence and context.

practice.prompt: Explain one implication of “crept” in the original sentence “Morning light crept across the floor”.
hints: Consider how the verb presents movement.
solution: “Crept” suggests slow, gradual movement.
Applied to light, it makes the changing illumination seem like a cautious advancing presence.

practice.prompt: Compare “requested” with the hypothetical replacement “demanded” in the original sentence “She requested a reply”.
hints: Do not claim the replacement is in the source.
solution: “Requested” presents asking without necessarily asserting force.
“Demanded” would imply a stronger insistence or claimed entitlement.
The original word leaves more room for a measured interaction, though wider context could change its tone.

practice.prompt: Analyse the vocabulary pattern in this original line: “He calculated each favour, counted each visit, and called the friendship a debt.”
hints: Which area of meaning connects the verbs and noun?
solution: “Calculated”, “counted” and “debt” form a pattern of accounting or financial language.
The pattern frames friendship as measured obligation rather than spontaneous exchange.
It supports a transactional portrayal here without proving that all the character’s relationships are the same.

practice.prompt: Original line: “He rescued the last biscuit.” Compare “rescued” with “took”.
solution: “Took” would report acquisition neutrally.
“Rescued” treats the biscuit as if it faced danger or loss.
The exaggerated importance can create humour, depending on the surrounding tone.
successCriteria: “Rescued” treats the biscuit as if it faced danger or loss.
The exaggerated importance can create humour, depending on the surrounding tone.

practice.prompt: Original line: “The rumour seeped through the school.” Explain the verb’s contribution.
hints: Think about gradual movement of liquid.
solution: “Seeped” suggests slow movement through small openings.
The rumour appears to spread indirectly rather than by one public announcement.
The image can imply difficulty containing it without proving who began it.
successCriteria: “Seeped” suggests slow movement through small openings.
The rumour appears to spread indirectly rather than by one public announcement.
The image can imply difficulty containing it without proving who began it.

notes.title: Diction in context
paragraphs: Diction is the selection of words and the associations they bring. Denotation concerns a word’s core meaning; connotation concerns further suggestions in context. Compare close alternatives to explain the precision of a verb or adjective. Snatched, took and received can describe possession changing hands while presenting different kinds of agency and force. Register also matters: formal, colloquial or technical wording shapes the relationship with an audience. Avoid treating a dictionary definition as the whole analysis; connect the chosen word to the passage’s action, voice and argument.

workedExamples.prompt: Original line: “She rationed her smiles during the interview.” Analyse “rationed”.
steps: The verb usually suggests limiting a scarce supply.
Applied to smiles, it makes friendliness seem controlled and deliberately distributed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The diction suggests careful self-presentation rather than spontaneous warmth.

flashcards.back: A word’s core or literal meaning.
Associations a word brings beyond its core meaning in context.
Their differences reveal the particular force of the chosen word.
A level or style of language associated with a situation or relationship.

nodes.detail: Smiles seem managed rather than spontaneous.

edges.label: The ordinary use of the verb supplies an association.
